reasoning: Colloquial 'cough' is geminated: ku77a/ku77e. ح is not in the back/emphatic list, so taa marbuta is written e; the final vowel is the uncertain part.
Everyday word, so ق is a glottal stop. The ف is doubled and taa marbuta after ف is e. A basket, also used for a produce crate.
Plain CVCC noun with no vowel changes. Standard word for sand.
Word-initial آ is a vowel seat, so it is written aa with no apostrophe. Phone greeting used everywhere, including Ramallah. Short-a 'allo' is a possible variant.

meaning_fix: It's as if you hadn't spoken / you might as well not have said anything (what you said had no effect or made no difference)
reasoning: The idiom literally means 'as if you hadn't spoken', from كأنّك. It only means 'you should have kept quiet' when the remark made things worse; the standard phrase for that is يا ريتك ما حكيت. The vowel in ka'innak/ki'innak varies.
MSA-origin religious word that Palestinians use in conversation. The final hamza is written '; some speakers drop it.
Relative illi, initial hamza vowel seat, then the bi- present prefix. The 3rd-person y is elided in city speech, so bi7ibb. Proverb equivalent to 'Love me, love my dog'.
خلص is 'finished', with emphatic S. عليّ is 3alayy. Reads as 'it's over for me'. With a doubled l (khallaS 3alayy) it would mean 'he finished me off'.
Past 3rd masc. sing. of فلت, 'slipped away or escaped'. Everyday Palestinian verb.
MSA-origin word in normal Palestinian use. ظ is written TH per the scheme. 'Conservative' is right; the same word also means 'governor' (e.g. of Ramallah).
The ID card is commonly called hawiyye in Palestine. The abstract sense 'identity' is sometimes said huwiyye. Taa marbuta after ي is e, and the ي is doubled.
Past kaanu plus bi- imperfect, with -u for 'they' and no final alif sound. City Palestinian elides the y: bil3abu (byil3abu is also heard). برا is barra with a doubled r.
MSA-origin sports term that is used in Palestinian conversation and news; colloquially 'boks' is also said. Taa marbuta after م is e.
Spoken Palestinian is urubba/awrubba, with a doubled b and no p. The spelling أروبا suggests urubba. Initial hamza is a vowel seat.
'Greeted' is the doubled form sallam (sallam 3ala = greeted or gave regards to). The English meaning rules out salim and salam.
English loan 'group', said with g, written here with غ (also spelled جروب). Real غروب means sunset (ghuruub). Safer glossed as 'group'; 'group chat' is the main modern use. TTS may read غ as gh.
ق in yiwaffi'ak is a glottal stop in this everyday blessing. بالشغل assimilates to bish-shughul, and Palestinian shughul has u in both syllables.
Palestinian monophthongises ay to ee: gheer, not ghayr. Means other or different, and also 'other than'.

meaning_fix: I missed you (to m.); to a woman say وحشتيني wa7ashtiini
reasoning: As spelled, without ي, this is the masculine-addressee form. The feminine form is وحشتيني. It is used in Palestine but is Egyptian-influenced; the native Palestinian way is اشتقتلك (ishta'tilak, f. ishta'tilik).
ثاني is respelled تاني because Palestinians say taani, not thaani. Literally 'I mean, in another sense', used as 'in other words'; 'bi-kalaam taani' is also said.
Loan from 'service', the normal word for a shared taxi in Palestine. The exact vowels and f versus v vary between speakers; written with f and long ii following the Arabic spelling.

meaning_fix: hit / knocked / rang (e.g. Ta'' il-baab = knocked on the door); also 'popped' or 'showed up suddenly'
reasoning: Doubled final ق is a glottal stop, giving Ta''. The core senses are to hit, knock or pop; 'went' is only a loose fit for sudden arrival.
More elevated than everyday jabhe, but common in sayings and affectionate phrases such as a kiss on the forehead, so it counts as Palestinian. Long ii in the second syllable.
Formal-origin but very common in everyday Palestinian (police or other interrogations). Both ق are glottal stops in urban speech.
Loan word used in Palestine alongside is3aaf. Stress falls on the final heavy syllable, so the vowels are short, as in English and Hebrew. The spelling's و and ا may be read long by some speakers.
